note: Healthy rats, dogs and rhesus dosed in their active phase carried every orexin antagonist into insomnia trials; orexin-deficient narcolepsy framed the safety question.
label: Insomnia (orexin)

engagement.model: Rat and dog sleep EEG/EMG in the active phase
engagement.note: Almorexant, a non-member DORA, cut wake and raised NREM/REM sleep in rats and dogs; its human arm does not score here.
engagement.short: Rat and dog EEG sleep; sibling drug
engagement.quote: Here we report that in rats, dogs and humans, somnolence is induced by pharmacological blockade of both orexin OX(1) and OX(2) receptors.
engagement.judgement: The rat/dog sleep-EEG model opens with almorexant, which is not a member of this class, so product_in_model is false and the paper's healthy-volunteer arm cannot score; the model itself is the one Merck reused for suvorexant (Winrow 2011).

engagement.magnitude_basis: PSG sleep efficiency/WASO vs animal active-wake time
engagement.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading of both papers (Europe PMC); comparison is my pairing.
engagement.model: Rat, dog and rhesus sleep EEG/EMG (suvorexant)
engagement.note: Suvorexant promoted PSG sleep in healthy men at 10-100 mg, as it cut active wake in rats, dogs and rhesus.
engagement.short: Healthy men slept more, as animals did
engagement.quote: Statistically significant sleep-promoting effects were observed with all doses of suvorexant compared to placebo.
engagement.reason: Human PSG sleep moved as animal EEG did
engagement.judgement: No human orexin-receptor PET tracer exists, so the engagement readout is the one the model used: EEG-defined sleep after a dose (downstream). I paired Winrow 2011 (suvorexant in rat, dog, rhesus, the EEG package the FDA pharmacology review lists) with the healthy-volunteer PSG study rather than with Herring 2012 (patients, Nov 2012), to keep engagement apart from the efficacy endpoint; dated by Sun 2013. Partial: animals showed more slow-wave/delta sleep, but Sun found no significant effect on EEG delta power.

dose.model: Rat/dog/rhesus EEG dose-response with ex-vivo OX2R occupancy in hOX2R rats
dose.note: Rat OX2R occupancy >90% at 1.1 uM plasma; the EEG data set a human target of C4h above 0.4 uM.
dose.short: Animal EEG sets a 0.4 uM plasma target
dose.quote: Examination of Suvorexant in radioligand binding assays using tissue from transgenic rats expressing the human OX(2)R found nearly full receptor occupancy (>90%) at plasma exposures of 1.1 μM.
dose.judgement: The 0.4 uM C4h target 'based on preclinical EEG data' is stated in the FDA clinical-pharmacology review, not in Winrow 2011; Winrow is the first public use of the suvorexant dose model.

dose.magnitude_basis: lowest effective dose (10 mg) vs lowest dose reaching the preclinical C4h target (40 mg)
dose.confidence_note: FDA reviews read in full text from the local bundle; patient dose-response from the FDA summary review and Herring 2012 abstract.
dose.model: Rat/dog/rhesus EEG dose-response with ex-vivo OX2R occupancy in hOX2R rats
dose.note: The 0.4 uM target was reached only at 40 mg and above; patients responded down to 10 mg, so the target was enough but about 4x high.
dose.quote: The target concentration for C4hr on day 14 was attained at doses ranging from 40 mg to 100 mg (attainment of the target is based on the lower bound of the CI)
dose.judgement: Scored same under the table row 'reached, drug worked': Phase 3 dosed 40 mg (30 mg elderly) to the target and it worked. But the FDA summary review found suvorexant 'effective ... at doses of 10 mg, 15 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg, 40 mg, and 80 mg' and the driving studies found 15 mg 'the only suvorexant dose, which did not cause next-day impairment', so the sponsor withdrew 30/40 mg. The model over-stated the needed exposure (~4x by dose, 10 vs 40 mg), and that overshoot is what the FDA cut. A re-scorer who reads the next-day impairment at the target dose as decision 16 toxicity could make this contra; I did not, because the model stated no tolerability margin for next-day effects. Gotter 2013 (rat 65% occupancy scaled to 0.33 uM) is a post-Phase-2b revision and is not used.

dose.magnitude_basis: dog NOAEL Cmax/AUC vs human Cmax/AUC at 50 mg (3x margin)
dose.confidence_note: FDA integrated review read in full text from the local bundle; registry dates for NCT03545191/NCT03575104 not looked up.
dose.note: Dog cataplexy NOAEL gave a 3-fold margin over the 50 mg maximum dose; no cataplexy appeared at 50 mg in Phase 3.
dose.quote: Although the safety margin is relatively small, no cataplexy was observed at the MRHD in phase 3 and long-term extension clinical studies.
dose.reason: Stated tolerability margin held in patients
dose.judgement: Decision 16 entry: the dog study stated a tolerated exposure (NOAEL 20 mg/kg/day, 3x the 50 mg MRHD by Cmax and AUC) and patients were dosed to 50 mg without that toxicity; cataplexy-like reactions appeared only at a supratherapeutic 200 mg. A different model from the suvorexant PK target, hence model_change. The FDA review puts both sides together, so comparison_stated is true.

efficacy.model: Rat and dog sleep EEG/EMG in the active phase
efficacy.note: Healthy rats and dogs dosed in their active phase; no animal model of insomnia itself. First used with sibling almorexant.
efficacy.short: Healthy rats and dogs, no insomnia model
efficacy.quote: When administered orally during the active period of the circadian cycle, a dual antagonist increased, in rats, electrophysiological indices of both non-REM and, particularly, REM sleep, in contrast to GABA(A) receptor modulators
efficacy.judgement: Almorexant is not a member, so product_in_model is false and its 2012 insomnia trial (Hoever 2012) does not score. Suvorexant entered the same model in Winrow 2011.

efficacy.magnitude_basis: PSG sleep efficiency vs animal active-wake time
efficacy.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading (Europe PMC); comparison is my pairing.
efficacy.model: Rat, dog and rhesus sleep EEG/EMG (suvorexant)
efficacy.note: Suvorexant raised PSG sleep efficiency dose-dependently in 254 primary-insomnia patients, as it promoted sleep in three species.
efficacy.short: Insomnia patients slept more, as predicted
efficacy.quote: Suvorexant showed significant (p values <0.01) dose-related improvements vs placebo on the coprimary end points of sleep efficiency at night 1 and end of week 4.
efficacy.reason: Primary endpoint moved as animals predicted
efficacy.judgement: My pairing of Herring 2012 with Winrow 2011; the trial does not cite the animal data. Not neg: no member has failed a primary endpoint in insomnia. Filorexant's Phase 2 (Connor 2016, doi:10.1093/ijnp/pyw022) was positive on sleep efficiency at all doses; it was dropped for portfolio reasons. Lemborexant, daridorexant, vornorexant and fazamorexant later met their primaries per their regulators/sponsors (not individually re-read). Dated by epub 2012-11-28; results posted 2014-11-14.

safety.model: Rat and dog dosing watched for cataplexy, against orexin-deficient narcolepsy
safety.note: Orexin loss causes narcolepsy-cataplexy in dogs, mice and people; acute almorexant gave no cataplexy in rats or dogs.
safety.short: Narcolepsy genetics flag cataplexy; none seen
safety.quote: No signs of cataplexy were observed, in contrast to the rodent, dog or human narcolepsy syndromes.
safety.judgement: Sibling drug (almorexant, non-member), so product_in_model is false and nothing scores until a member's animal and patient data meet.

safety.magnitude_basis: presence of cataplexy-like events at high dose
safety.confidence_note: FDA medical, pharmacology review and label read in full text from the local bundle.
safety.model: Dog repeat dosing with food-enrichment cataplexy trigger (suvorexant)
safety.note: Dogs on 30 mg/kg suvorexant buckled on food enrichment; patients on 40-80 mg had cataplexy-like leg weakness; the label warns it rises with dose.
safety.short: Dog cataplexy matched mild patient events
safety.quote: I conclude that the episode was clearly cataplexy-like, as brief leg weakness occurring when laughing is classic for cataplexy in narcoleptics
safety.reason: Dog cataplexy signal recurred in patients
safety.judgement: The review sets the nonclinical finding ('nonclinical studies suggested a theoretical safety concern for cataplexy') beside the patient cases, so comparison_stated is true. The sponsor's adjudication found no confirmed cataplexy; the CDTL overruled that for one patient and listed others at 40-80 mg, and the label (5.6) warns of dose-related cataplexy-like symptoms. Daridorexant (2022) and lemborexant (2019, one adjudicated event; mouse chocolate-cataplexy model) agree. Next-day impairment, the harm behind the FDA dose cut, was not tested in the animal package; I score it under dose, not here.
